posts.title: Lego MOC SF90 Stradale 1:8 Technic SuperSportCar (by Lox Lego)
posts.text: How a passion for 1:8 supercars turned into an incredible collaboration It all started back in 2017, when I stumbled across the LEGO Technic 42056 Porsche 911 GT3 RS in a toy store. That moment reignited my childhood passion for LEGO and marked the beginning of what would become a real obsession with LEGO Technic 1:8 supercars. As I explored the world of modern LEGO Technic builds, I discovered Rebrickable - and with it, an entirely new universe of incredible fan-designed creations, known as MOCs (My Own Creations). Two models immediately caught my attention: the McLaren P1 by brunojj1 and the Ford GT by Lox Lego. These became the first two MOCs I ever built, and they opened the door to a whole new level of LEGO Technic building. From there, my collection - and my enthusiasm - continued to grow. Next came brunojj1's stunning Ferrari 488 Pista in white and blue modification, followed by two more creations from Lox Lego: a striking yellow Ferrari F12 and a beautiful red-and-gold Ferrari Testarossa. At that point, I was already hooked. But I had no idea that my passion for building these models would eventually lead to something much bigger. February 2023 – The Beginning of Something Special In February 2023, Lox Lego started sharing a few teasers of his upcoming Ferrari F40. For me, this was a big deal. The F40 has always been one of my all-time favorite cars - easily in my personal top three. Naturally, I couldn't resist reaching out to Lox. I was absolutely determined to be among the first people to build his new creation. Somehow, that initial contact turned into a genuine connection. During the build, I discovered a few errors in the parts list (yes, I tend to notice these things! 😄). What started as a simple exchange about missing or incorrect parts gradually developed into a closer collaboration. From Builder to Development Support With my engineering background, a keen eye for detail, and what I would describe as a rather extensive knowledge of LEGO Technic parts, I found myself in a position to contribute more actively to Lox's projects. One of the most exciting opportunities came during the development of his Audi RS6. Being a huge fan of Audi - my favorite automotive brand - having the chance to build and support the development of a prototype RS6 was something truly special. I was no longer simply following instructions and assembling a finished design. I was becoming involved in the development process itself, helping to identify potential improvements and contributing feedback from a builder's perspective. And the journey didn't stop there. I subsequently had the opportunity to participate in test builds of the Porsche 911 (992) GT3 R and the Hennessey Venom F5 Revolution. For the Hennessey, I was even able to contribute my own prototype seat design - a small but personally rewarding step from being a test builder toward becoming an active design contributor. September 2024 – The Ferrari SF90 Project In September 2024, another exciting chapter began: the development of Lox Lego's Ferrari SF90. Unlike the previous projects, the SF90 was originally intended to become a commercially released building set in cooperation with a third-party company. Once again, I was given the fantastic opportunity to participate in the prototype and test-building phase. But this time, I decided to take things a little further. Why build just one prototype when you can build two? It sounded like a great idea at the time - although handling more than 8,000 LEGO pieces simultaneously certainly made me question that decision more than once! 😄 The plan was to create two distinct versions of the SF90 and I instantly collected the parts from my collection. posts.text: I remember my post on the 2024 thread stating I thought it was a weak year simply because I was annoyed things like the Jedi games were still being ignored. Amusing how wrong I was in retrospect, the amount of variety and solid playsets it gave us were phenomenal. If I had to rank the ‘modern’ era of the theme from 2021 onwards, it would probably look like this: 1. (Tie) 2024 for an all-round solid lineup of playsets, including the introduction of well-executed location sets which Star Wars had not seen in a long time. 1. (Tie) 2021 for the variety and excellent set choices. They clearly knew what people wanted from current shows like the Mandalorian, TCW, and TBB. 2. 2022 because it was full of winners like the AT-TE, Scythe, Ambush on Ferrix, etc. 3. 2023 for the Ahsoka wave. That wave single-handedly redeemed the year after a very weak January and August wave although it also gave the best diorama (Throne Room Duel) as well. 4. 2025 was a bit of a downer because of the excessive focus on TCW or at least the ‘clone’ part, but it also introduced the GOATed £60 - £65 price-point which gave us the ARC-170, U-Wing Jango’s Slave I, and V-19. Of course with this price-point being the best we’ve seen in the line, it lost much of its prominent in 2026. Shout-out to the UCS Slave I as well. 5. 2026 with the triple-whammy of a singular focus on Mandalorian, introduction of Smart Play, and newfound trend of Lego beginning to completely disregard new Star Wars shows like Maul: Shadow Lord which has set a depressing precedent for the theme in the years to come. However the Remnant AT-AT, Offworld Sandcrawler, and Cobb Vanth’s Speeder were all phenomenal. Looking at the above, I think the theme is undergoing that perfect storm of an increase in non-playsets, reduced playset slots, a further dilution of playset slots because of Smart Play, and a severe crackdown in overall variety across Star Wars media. Next year at least improves on the variety aspect. But on a more positive note, even the weak years have introduced positive changes too. The flagship playsets this year are the best they’ve been in a long time, last year introduced the perfect price-point for ships with a solid complement of minifigures, etc. etc.

posts.text: Unfortunately: Not really. The problematic term is "anything" . Some "things" that can make light, can in fact send IR commands or messages to an RCX - however these need to fulfil a number of requisites ... IR = infra-red; infra (latin) = below, underneath; so your light source needs to produce light below red = not visible light. Light = electromagnetic radiation. Visible light (from red to violet) is only a >tiny< fraction of the entire spectrum of electromagnetic radiation, we know so far. Below red = infra red (and so much more), above violet = ultra violet (and so much more ...). Red has a larger wavelength (800 nm = less energy) than violet (350 nm). The translucent red cap won't do anything other than letting red light pass through. Most translucent plastic materials are transparent for infrared light as well. But you need to generate infrared light in the first place. These translucent red windows/caps are mostly used to get a smooth outside surface, as most people like that. An IR source is usually - less nice. For some ... I like them . Light sources are e.g., incandescent light bulbs, such as the 9V lamps. There is a tiny filament inside and depending on its temperature, it emits a broad spectrum of visible and mostly infrared light when it glows. So you could conclude that a 9V lamp is a good source for playing with an RCX - but unfortunately it is not, because the RCX IR sensor is sensitive only to IR radiation that is "pulsed". You can shine a strong, continuously emitting IR light source onto an RCX and it won't do anything. You need to turn on and off the IR light 38000 times per second or 38kHz. Then the RCX detector "sees" that light. The thing is: The glowing filament inside the 9V lamp is way "too slow" - when you turn the power off, it will still glow for some time. So what people use instead are IR light emitting diodes (LEDs), and these are used in the serial and USB IR tower for the RCX as well. LEDs react rapidly to power changes, as the light generating process is not thermal, as in the 9V bulb, but through electronic excitation processes - and these are really fast, much faster than 38 kHz. IR LEDs emit radiation in a narrow infrared light window of the electromagnetic spectrum, so most of the electrical energy supplied to an IR LED is actually used to generate defined IR wavelengths. You can select from many such IR LEDs, which emit at different wavelengths. The RCX uses IR light at 940 ... 950 nm (well below visible light) and there are numerous cheap IR LEDs available for that wavelength. Most probably any IR remote you own (TV etc.) uses the same wavelength. That is the reason, @Bliss' ESP32 PFIR gateway can "see" the codes of many generic IR remotes. And finally, the RCX talks to the world using packages of IR light. Each packet consists of a number of "bits" (0/1) where 1 = on = 38000 pulses/second, 0 = off = no IR pulses at all). These come in to the RCX or are sent out at by the RCX a rate of 2400 bits/s = 2400 Baud. I believe that the Interface B can't turn on/off its outputs that fast (other than at fixed pulse width modulated rates for power 1-7 settings, that need to match the 38kHz restriction - but this is certainly not the case). In conclusion: No, it won't work with an Int.B + 9V lamp (or even IR LED) ... Yes, this is what people have done, I know for sure the LEGO train folks, when they use PF (which is also using an IR bit protocol, at 38kHz modulation). Problem with IR is that you need a line of sight (or reflections) to the detector. I believe a good number of these folks use PoweredUp nowadays. PUp is also emitting electromagnetic radiation, but at much lower frequencies than IR, in the microwave range (GHz). That radiation penetrates matter much, much easier than IR and so you don't need a line of sight ... Hope that helps. Best Thorsten

posts.title: [MOC] Corridor Clocker
posts.text: I have always been fascinated by the 90s/2000s lego train sets. Specifically, the santa fe and the metroliner. I think it is great that back in the day lego sold x-in-1 kits of trains (like santa fe, my own train etc) that you can customize and basically build a train with, but also just something about the metroliner set has a special charm that I have no idea how to explain it. Nevertheless, I never had the opportunity to get the set, and now its a bit too late is it. So why not try to capture the essence of them by "combining" the concepts into one, into something straight out of early amtrak? So, I present to you my WIP project, the Clocker. Its been a year since I started it with a huge hiatus in the middle, but I'm finally showing this to everyone. I took a bit of creative liberty to make it look pleasing in lego while still resembling the real prototype. For example, these cars in real life would have curved roofs, but that wasn't feasible unless I made the cars a bit taller, which did throw the proportions off. So, I made the roof with 45 degree slopes, which still alludes to the "metroliner" lego design. Some color variation was used to break the otherwise monotone grey body. The chassis is lengthened by 8 studs, but it is still 6 studs wide. It is designed to be affordable enough to be a "consist-builder," so its aimed to be on the cheaper side. It was about $50-60 per car on BrickLink, but I am not sure what the benchmark is for individual cars these days so you can be the judge. So far, I have made two variants of coach cars (ex-Penn Central & ex-Southern Pacific), a diner car, and a parlor car. Interior for some of the cars (ex-Penn Central coach, ex-Southern Pacific coach, ex-Penn Central parlor). The dining car's interior is still work in progress. Phase III version for those interested. Now, I am also in the process of building a loco to pull the consist, and what better representative is there other than an E60? I am planning to make other variants, suggestions and feedback are welcome!

posts.title: LEGO Ninjago Ongoing Rumours and Discussion
posts.text: Solid take and one I agree with. Themes like Ninjago and City are the perfect sandbox for truly testing the value added to the traditional play experience by Smart Play. The amount of money that’s been sunk into the Smart Brick and the manner in which it’s been marketed as an absolute game changer for Lego means that right now it’s far too big to fail (even if factors such as the abysmal sales for Star Wars’ Smart Play sets are there). It was inevitable that Ninjago would be touched by it. The only thing I’m surprised about is just how many smart sets they’re doing for Ninjago. Moreover, we have seen time and time again that the Ninjago designers are some of the best employed by Lego. I have far more faith in their ability to figure out a thoughtful way to integrate the Smart Brick into playsets than Star Wars did so I’m sure their implementation of it will go beyond some rudimentary use of colour-coded pieces and simple mechanisms to make the Smart Brick move and react accordingly. All that said…my collecting scope for Ninjago is far smaller than it used to be with me primarily focusing on the Legends sets, so I also feel less invested in the Dragons Rising / Fury stuff. Ivo’s Dojo alone already seems like it scratches my Ninjago itch for 2027. Nonetheless, whilst I don’t have high hopes for what Smart Play will look like for Ninjago, I have no doubt it’ll be executed far better than in Star Wars. I’m just looking forward to seeing the remaining Legends sets, the Earth Mech Unit sounds pretty cool and it seems like Ivo’s Dojo will have some play functions to it - I can’t wait to see what Master Zane looks like!

posts.text: @Bliss Other random ideas The DevKit 1 boards have ample of GPIOs available when using them as LEGO Blockly servers, gateways/bridges. The ESP32 PFIR gateway provides 38kHz modulated PF signals for directly driving LEDs or power amplifiers (transistors, FETs etc.). That is perfect! How about exposing the non-modulated, direct digital PF signals on another GPIO? Reasoning: You could use other means of signal transport than IR, particularly RF. In this post I described how I did that - others may find alternative approaches as well. The RF transport just extends the range for PF to non-line-of-sight. This worked also very well with the RC Trains chassis - I can't find the photos right now ... You have implemented the IR RCCar protocoll (you call IRC) in the "RC/CM" tab, subtab "USB Tower", USB Tower option "USB Tower mode": IRC. ICR is applying to the NitroFlash cars - but also to the Bionicle "Manas" controllers, as well as to Spybotics. I believe these could be also readily implemented into the ESP32 PFIR gateway - making this ESP a "LEGO IR" gateway. The IR RC train protocol goes along the same line. Again, one ESP can handle them all, just give these protocols an ID and the ESP would send out the appropriate protocol? This is just adhering to the current ESP32 PFIR gateway, which could be a general IR gateway for (unidirectional) PF, RCCar (NitroFlash, Manas, Spybotics), RCTrain protocols. The gateway could provide the 38kHz modulated as well as the digital data signals. And of course read the IR remote signals. Maybe that is overkill ... And yes, this is mocking my MulPI approach, but with LEGO Blockly access! Just speculating. I believe you like challenges ... Best Thorsten

posts.text: If you are interested, I have some NQC as well as RobotC programs, where I applied multitasking and the like for my train layout. RobotC came out of NQC but performs much faster on an RCX. The syntax is rather similar if not identical. In earlier NQC guides you may find byte codes referring to the Swan firmware, It was Dick Swan who initially delivered (free) firmwares for the RCX, which were NQC compatible. I believe I still have those somewhere. Later they separated. However, RobotC for the RCX is available for free as legacy version, as they don't update stuff for the RCX anymore (since long). Back in the days, Dave Baum, author of NQC implemented short jumps, just because I was shy of about 10 bytes in my NQC code for Scouts operating switch point controllers ... as you know, the Scouts only have 396 byte code memory. On an RCX this is not an issue, as it is a 8kbyte memory monster. I contacted Dave, he said why not, and since then NQC decides whether a long jump is necessary of a short will do. A long jump eats away 5 bytes, a short only 3! And as there are usually some jumps in a multitasking program, they add up . My RCX operated (9V) trains use NQC (without PID speed control) as well as RobotC (with PID controlled speed control) as an example. Same for my switch point controllers (RCX/Scout). Just let me know and I can try to dig some stuff out. Best Thorsten
